text: A data catalog is a searchable inventory of an organization's data assets — tables, reports, dashboards, files — that pulls together business and technical metadata from multiple sources into one place someone can actually search.
Where the glossary covers business terms and the dictionary covers physical structures, the catalog is the layer that surfaces both together, plus usage information neither of them tracks on its own.

Lesson 5 warned about repository sprawl. A poorly designed catalog just adds a fourth place metadata has to be separately maintained. A well-designed catalog instead pulls from the others — reading business definitions from the glossary, structural metadata from the dictionary, lineage from pipeline tools.

A catalog entry surfaces three things together. What it is — the technical structure from the dictionary. What it means — the business definition from the glossary. And how it's actually used — which reports query this table, how often, by whom. That third one is what makes a catalog genuinely different from a glossary and dictionary stapled together.

This is the practical resolution to Lesson 5's sprawl problem — a catalog that actually integrates, rather than becoming its own fourth silo. Next lesson: catalog capabilities and search — what makes a catalog actually usable, not just comprehensive.
